error_modes.label: Formation T/O - takeoff airspeed at rotation and lift-off

texts.0: SP, due to a rotation input made on the runway picture rather than on the airspeed indication, did not execute the formation T/O with the standard takeoff airspeed. The aircraft was rotated below the computed speed, against a criterion that allows no tolerance on the low side, and the airspeed then overshot the standard by more than 10 knots while SP chased the attitude. IP intervened on the controls to set the takeoff attitude and to restore the standard airspeed before the departure turn.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that remained on the runway and on No2 and reached the airspeed indication late, did not hold the standard takeoff airspeed during the formation T/O. The excess settled at about 10 knots, at the outer limit of the allowed one-sided tolerance, and was reduced only after two verbal calls from IP. The fast condition was carried into the initial climb and obliged No2 to add power to hold position.
texts.2: SP, due to a rotation input applied slightly later than the computed speed required, allowed the takeoff airspeed to build past the standard by roughly 7 knots, between the code 3 and code 1 limits. SP identified the excess on the indicator and reset the takeoff attitude on his own initiative before the first turn. No prompting and no IP control input were required and No2 held position throughout.
texts.3: SP executed the formation T/O with the standard takeoff airspeed, rotating on the computed speed with no deviation on the low side and holding the excess inside 5 knots. The scan alternated continuously between the runway, the airspeed indication and No2, and the pitch corrections were small and immediate.
texts.4: SP rotated precisely at the computed takeoff speed and held the standard airspeed through lift-off and the transition to the climb, with deviations that were negligible against the published tolerance. The speed was stabilized so smoothly that No2 needed only minimal power changes to remain in position.
texts.marginal: SP kept the takeoff airspeed within standards but consistently on the fast side of the target, with the excess sitting close to the code 3 figure for most of the initial climb. The trend did not exceed tolerance and did not displace No2, but it left little margin for a power correction on the wing. SP is expected to set the computed speed exactly at rotation and to hold it during the next formation takeoffs.

texts_at.1: SP executed the formation T/O with the takeoff airspeed reaching about 10 knots above standard, at the tolerance limit, because the rotation input was applied a beat later than the computed speed called for. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to move the rotation cue earlier so the airspeed excess comes down from the edge of the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP held the formation T/O airspeed to roughly 7 knots above standard, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the pitch correction at rotation was slightly softer than the computed speed required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to firm up the rotation input so the airspeed settles closer to the standard.
texts_at.3: SP flew the formation T/O within 5 knots of the standard takeoff airspeed on three of the four repetitions, with the fourth affected by a rotation started a fraction late while the scan was still settling on No2. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to bring the scan to the airspeed indicator earlier in the roll so every repetition matches the first three.

texts_above.2: SP rotated at the computed speed and held the formation T/O airspeed within roughly 7 knots of standard, catching the small excess on the indicator and resetting the takeoff attitude without prompting. Tightening the scan between the runway and the airspeed indication in the first seconds of the roll would trim even that margin. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound power and pitch coordination at rotation.
texts_above.3: SP rotated on the computed speed and kept the formation T/O airspeed inside 5 knots of standard on every repetition, with the scan alternating continuously between the runway, the airspeed indication and No2. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good power and pitch coordination at rotation.
texts_above.4: SP rotated precisely at the computed speed and held the formation T/O airspeed within a knot or two of standard through lift-off and the transition to the climb, so No2 needed only minimal power changes to stay in position. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent power and pitch coordination at rotation.

error_modes.label: Formation T/O - runway line tracking during the takeoff roll
error_modes.source: specific:Maintain in the center line of RWY (ft)

texts.0: SP, due to rudder input insufficient for the yaw produced at power application and for the reported crosswind, did not maintain the assigned takeoff line during the formation T/O roll. Lateral displacement passed 10 feet and continued to diverge toward the half of the runway occupied by No2, reducing the lateral separation of the pair. IP took the controls to re-establish the takeoff track before rotation.
texts.1: SP, due to directional corrections applied in discrete steps instead of continuously, did not maintain the assigned takeoff line during the formation T/O roll. Displacement reached about 10 feet, at the limit of the allowed deviation, and the aircraft was re-centered only after IP called for rudder. The pair lifted off with the track still offset and with No2 correcting to preserve spacing.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow initial response to the swing at power application, drifted off the assigned takeoff line by roughly 8 feet. The deviation stayed between the code 3 and code 1 limits and SP corrected it with coordinated rudder well before rotation, without prompting and without IP action. Lateral separation from No2 was never in question.
texts.3: SP maintained the aircraft on the assigned takeoff line during the formation T/O with lateral deviation held inside 5 feet. Rudder inputs were continuous and matched to the yaw produced by power application and by the crosswind, and the same track was carried through rotation and lift-off.
texts.4: SP held the aircraft on the assigned takeoff line with deviations barely perceptible against the runway markings, anticipating the yaw rather than reacting to it. The track was preserved unchanged into the initial climb and gave No2 a stable reference for the whole roll.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft inside the lateral tolerance but with a persistent offset to one side that was held rather than removed for most of the ground roll. The offset stayed within standards and did not grow, but it consumed part of the lateral margin toward No2. SP is expected to re-center the aircraft as soon as the offset is recognized instead of accepting it for the remainder of the roll.

texts_at.1: SP held the formation T/O within about 10 feet of the takeoff line, at the tolerance limit, because the directional corrections were made in discrete steps rather than continuously as the swing developed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply rudder continuously through the swing so the deviation comes off the tolerance limit.
texts_at.2: SP tracked the formation T/O line within roughly 8 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the initial response to the swing at power application was a touch slow. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate the swing at power application so the drift is caught before it builds.
texts_at.3: SP held the takeoff line inside 5 feet on three repetitions, with one drifting slightly wider while rudder pressure was still being matched to a stronger gust. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to match rudder pressure to the reported crosswind before brake release rather than after the swing begins.

texts_above.2: SP drifted only about 8 feet off the takeoff line before catching it with coordinated rudder well before rotation, with no prompting needed. Centering the aircraft at the first sign of the swing, rather than after it, would close even that margin. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound rudder discipline on the takeoff line.
texts_above.3: SP held the formation T/O line inside 5 feet on every repetition, with rudder inputs continuous and matched to the yaw from power application and the crosswind alike. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed rudder discipline on the takeoff line.
texts_above.4: SP held the takeoff line with deviations barely perceptible against the runway markings, anticipating the yaw rather than reacting to it and giving No2 an unchanging reference for the whole roll. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional rudder discipline on the takeoff line.

error_modes.label: Formation T/O - factors considered in placing No2 on the correct side

texts.0: SP, due to retention of the briefed mental model after the active runway and the direction of the departure turn had changed, did not take into consideration the essential factors for placing No2 on the correct side. No2 was assigned the side inside the departure turn and downwind of the reported crosswind, which put him low and closing on the leader during the initial turn. IP directed a change of formation position and assumed the lead of the departure.
texts.1: SP, due to a mental model of the departure that was not updated when the takeoff data changed, assigned No2 a side that did not account for the crosswind and for the first turn. The error was recognized and stated only after IP questioned the takeoff briefing on the ground, and the assignment was changed on IP prompting rather than on SP initiative. The correction was made in time but left the pair rushed at the line up.
texts.2: SP, due to a mental model of the departure that was reassessed only after the clearance was read back, initially named No2 on the side away from the wind. SP re-evaluated the crosswind, the direction of the first turn and the obstacle situation before line up and corrected the assignment on his own, so No2 was in fact placed on the correct side. The late reassessment cost part of the time available for the line up checks.
texts.3: SP took into consideration all the essential factors and placed No2 on the correct side, weighing the crosswind, the direction of the departure turn, the sun and the obstacle situation. The assignment was stated clearly in the takeoff briefing and required no change once the clearance was received.
texts.4: SP placed No2 on the correct side after an assessment that covered the crosswind, the departure turn, the terrain and the traffic, and stated the reasoning in the briefing so No2 shared the same picture. The assignment remained valid through the clearance and the takeoff without any adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP placed No2 on the correct side, but the decision rested mainly on the habitual side used in previous sorties and the supporting factors were named only when asked. The choice was appropriate for the conditions of the day, yet the reasoning behind it was not demonstrated. SP is expected to derive the side from wind, departure turn and obstacles on every takeoff briefing.

texts_at.1: SP placed No2 on the correct side for the formation T/O, but only after the IP's question about the crosswind and the first turn prompted a second look at the assignment made at the briefing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to weigh the crosswind and the turn direction unprompted, before the takeoff briefing is closed.
texts_at.2: SP reassessed the side assignment for No2 once, changing it after the takeoff clearance had already been read back, and reached the correct placement without further prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to settle the side assignment before the clearance is read back so no late change is needed.
texts_at.3: SP named the crosswind, the departure turn and the obstacle situation in the takeoff briefing and placed No2 correctly on that basis, needing no change once the clearance was received. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to add the sun position to the same briefing check so the full set of factors is covered by habit.

texts_above.2: SP placed No2 correctly after re-evaluating the crosswind and the first turn on the ramp, catching a side assignment that no longer fit the takeoff data before it reached the line. Naming the same factors once, at the original briefing, would remove the need for the second look. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid briefing judgment for the wingman side.
texts_above.3: SP weighed the crosswind, the departure turn, the sun and the obstacle situation together and placed No2 correctly at the first briefing, with the assignment requiring no change through the clearance and the takeoff. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed briefing judgment for the wingman side.
texts_above.4: SP worked out the wingman side from a complete assessment of wind, terrain and traffic and stated the reasoning clearly enough that No2 shared the same picture without a follow-up question. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding briefing judgment for the wingman side.

error_modes.label: Formation T/O - monitoring of No2 through the roll and lift-off

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted cross-check that stayed on his own instruments through the takeoff roll, did not effectively monitor No2 during the maneuver. The acceleration deficit and the lateral drift of No2 went unobserved, and at the same time the leader's own displacement from the assigned line passed 10 feet toward the wingman. IP called the deviation and took the controls to move the flight path away from No2.
texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check divided between the instruments and the runway with no place left for the wingman, did not effectively monitor No2 during the formation T/O. Scan of the wingman resumed only after two calls from IP, by which time the leader's own lateral deviation had reached about 10 feet at the limit of the allowed tolerance. The pair became airborne with the relative position corrected by No2 alone.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that reached the wingman late in the acceleration, monitored No2 only intermittently in the first part of the takeoff roll. The lapse allowed the leader's own line deviation to grow to roughly 8 feet, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before SP re-established the scan, re-centered the aircraft and resumed continuous monitoring of No2 without prompting.
texts.3: SP effectively monitored No2 during the maneuver, keeping the wingman inside a scan that also covered the runway, the airspeed and the engine indications. Deviations of No2 in acceleration and position were seen as they developed and were answered with small power and track adjustments by the leader.
texts.4: SP monitored No2 continuously from brake release to the establishment of the climb, integrating the wingman into the scan without any loss of precision on the leader's own parameters. Every deviation of No2 was recognized at onset and addressed with a leader input before it required any correction from the wingman.
texts.marginal: SP monitored No2 during the maneuver, but the checks on the wingman were spaced widely enough that the position was confirmed only at brake release and again at lift-off. Nothing was missed on this takeoff and all parameters stayed within standards, yet a deviation developing between those two points would not have been seen early. SP is expected to keep the wingman inside a continuous scan for the whole roll.

texts_at.1: SP resumed the scan of No2 only after being reminded, by which point the leader's own line deviation had reached about 10 feet, at the tolerance limit, because the cross-check had stayed on the runway and the engine instruments without a place for the wingman. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to fold No2 into the scan from brake release so the check does not need a reminder.
texts_at.2: SP let the leader's own line deviation grow to roughly 8 feet before the wingman scan reached its normal rate, because the cross-check took longer than planned to widen out from the runway and the engine indications. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to widen the scan to No2 earlier in the roll so the deviation does not build before it is checked.
texts_at.3: SP kept the leader's own line inside 5 feet while monitoring No2, with the scan reaching the wingman a little later than ideal on one of the four repetitions. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make the timing of the first wingman check as consistent as the other three.

texts_above.2: SP re-established the scan of No2 after a lapse of only a few seconds, with the leader's own line deviation held to about 8 feet while the check was recovered without prompting. Spacing the checks on No2 more evenly through the roll, rather than catching up after a gap, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady cross-check between the leader's own line and No2.
texts_above.3: SP kept the leader's own line inside 5 feet while a scan that also covered the runway, the airspeed and the engine indications caught every deviation of No2 as it developed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate cross-check between the leader's own line and No2.
texts_above.4: SP integrated No2 into the scan without any loss of precision on the leader's own line, catching every deviation of the wingman at onset and answering it with a leader input before No2 had to correct. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary cross-check between the leader's own line and No2.

error_modes.label: Formation T/O - gear retraction command after No2 is confirmed airborne

texts.0: SP, due to a command sequence run on the leader's own lift-off instead of on the state of the wingman, gave the command for landing gear retraction without confirming that No2 was safely airborne. No2 was still in the rotation and accepted the call with the aircraft in ground effect, and the leader's own airspeed was at the same time more than 10 knots above the standard. IP countermanded the call on the radio and took the controls to stabilize the departure.
texts.1: SP, due to a fixed cadence carried over from single-ship departures, gave the command for landing gear retraction before positively confirming that No2 was safely airborne. The call was corrected only after IP prompted for the wingman's state, and the leader's airspeed sat at about 10 knots above the standard while the exchange took place. The formation was reconfigured late and the departure turn was begun with the pair still settling.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the leader's own climb parameters, began the gear retraction call slightly before the check on No2 was complete. SP interrupted the call on his own initiative, confirmed visually that No2 was safely airborne and then passed the command, with the leader's airspeed excess reaching roughly 7 knots between the code 3 and code 1 limits during the pause. No prompting and no IP input were needed.
texts.3: SP confirmed that No2 was safely airborne before giving the command for landing gear retraction, checking the wingman's climb and position and only then passing the call. The command was clear, standard and timed so that the formation was clean before the departure turn.
texts.4: SP confirmed No2 safely airborne with a positive visual check and passed the gear retraction command at the exact point required, without interrupting the leader's own climb parameters. The formation was configured as a pair, on a stable flight path, and the departure turn was entered clean.
texts.marginal: SP confirmed that No2 was airborne before commanding gear retraction, but the confirmation was a quick glance rather than a positive check of the wingman's climb, and the call followed almost immediately. Nothing was missed on this takeoff, yet the margin between the check and the command was very small. SP is expected to complete the check on No2 deliberately before passing the command.

texts_at.1: SP passed the gear-up call only after the check on No2 was interrupted and restarted, with the leader's own airspeed sitting about 10 knots above standard at the tolerance limit while the exchange was sorted out, because the command cadence was still carried over from single-ship departures. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to build the positive check on No2 into the same rhythm as the climb, rather than treating it as a separate step.
texts_at.2: SP interrupted the gear-up call without prompting once the check on No2 was seen to be incomplete, with the leader's own airspeed excess reaching roughly 7 knots during the pause, because attention had settled on the leader's own climb parameters first. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the visual check on No2 before starting the call rather than during it.
texts_at.3: SP held the leader's own airspeed within 5 knots of standard while confirming No2 safely airborne before every gear-up call, with the confirmation itself brief rather than deliberate on one of the four departures. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make that one confirmation as unhurried as the other three.

texts_above.2: SP interrupted an early gear-up call to complete the check on No2, holding the leader's own airspeed excess to about 7 knots while the sequence was corrected without prompting. Confirming No2 airborne before starting the call, rather than during it, would remove that pause altogether. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable sequencing of the gear-up call.
texts_above.3: SP confirmed No2 safely airborne before every gear-up call, with the leader's own airspeed held inside 5 knots of standard through each check and no call needing a correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good sequencing of the gear-up call.
texts_above.4: SP passed the gear-up command at the exact point required, on a positive visual check of No2 that never interrupted the leader's own climb parameters, so every departure was configured clean before the turn. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior sequencing of the gear-up call.

error_modes.label: Interval T/O - takeoff airspeed at rotation and lift-off

texts.0: SP, due to an aft stick input applied without reference to the airspeed indication, did not execute the interval T/O with the standard takeoff airspeed. IP intervened on the controls to set the takeoff attitude and to recover the standard airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a late transition of the scan from the runway to the airspeed indication, did not hold the standard takeoff airspeed on the interval T/O. The excess settled at about 10 knots, at the outer limit of the one-sided tolerance, and was removed only after two verbal prompts from IP. The fast climb increased the separation from No2 and delayed the join-up.
texts.2: SP, due to a rotation input made slightly after the computed speed, allowed the takeoff airspeed to build past the standard by roughly 7 knots, between the code 3 and code 1 limits. SP saw the excess on the indicator and reset the takeoff attitude on his own initiative, restoring the planned climb speed before the departure turn. No prompting and no IP control input were required.
texts.3: SP executed the interval T/O with the standard takeoff airspeed, rotating on the computed speed with no deviation on the low side and holding the excess inside 5 knots. The airspeed was flown to the value that supported the planned interval and the join-up geometry.
texts.4: SP rotated precisely at the computed takeoff speed and held the standard airspeed through lift-off and the climb, with deviations negligible against the published tolerance. The precision of the speed gave No2 a predictable closure for the join-up without any power change by the leader.
texts.marginal: SP held the takeoff airspeed within standards but consistently on the fast side of the target, with the excess close to the code 3 figure through the initial climb. The deviation stayed inside tolerance, yet it slowly stretched the interval and left No2 with more closure work than planned. SP is expected to fly the exact climb speed so that the briefed spacing is preserved.

texts_at.1: SP held the interval T/O airspeed to about 10 knots above standard, at the tolerance limit, because the rotation input again landed a beat after the computed speed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the rotation cue forward so the climb starts closer to the standard speed.
texts_at.2: SP kept the interval T/O airspeed to roughly 7 knots above standard, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the pitch correction at rotation was slightly under-applied. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to firm up the rotation pitch so the excess airspeed comes down.
texts_at.3: SP held the interval T/O airspeed inside 5 knots of standard on three of the four departures, with the fourth affected by a rotation flown a fraction late. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to match the fourth rotation to the other three.

texts_above.2: SP reset the takeoff attitude without prompting once the interval T/O airspeed excess reached about 7 knots, restoring the planned climb speed before the departure turn. Rotating on the computed speed rather than a beat after it would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured speed control on the interval climb.
texts_above.3: SP held the interval T/O airspeed inside 5 knots of standard on every departure, flying the value that supported the planned interval and the join-up geometry throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise speed control on the interval climb.
texts_above.4: SP rotated at the computed speed and held the interval T/O airspeed within a knot or two of standard through the climb, giving No2 a predictable closure with no power change of the leader's own. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate speed control on the interval climb.

error_modes.label: Interval T/O - spacing and timing of brake release for the briefed interval

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit work into the last seconds before line up, did not take into consideration the essential factors that set the interval for No2. Brake release was made without regard to the crosswind side, the departure turn or the spacing briefed, and No2 was left with closure that could not be resolved on the departure path. IP directed a delay to No2 on the radio and took the aircraft to open the geometry.
texts.1: SP, due to workload management that left the line up checks unfinished until after the takeoff clearance, did not apply the briefed timing for the interval. Brake release was taken well outside the briefed spacing and was adjusted only after IP called for the correct interval, while the leader's own airspeed then ran about 10 knots above the standard in the climb. The join-up was flown with a geometry that No2 had to correct.
texts.2: SP, due to workload concentrated in the last part of the line up, initially set a brake release that did not match the briefed interval. SP recognized the discrepancy against the takeoff briefing, adjusted the timing on his own initiative and rolled with the planned spacing, with the resulting airspeed excess in the climb reaching roughly 7 knots between the code 3 and code 1 limits. No prompting and no IP action were needed.
texts.3: SP took into consideration the essential factors for the interval, weighing the crosswind side, the direction of the departure turn and the briefed spacing, and released brakes at the planned point. The interval produced by the takeoff matched the briefing and gave No2 a straightforward join-up.
texts.4: SP set the interval from a complete assessment of wind, departure turn and traffic, and released brakes exactly at the briefed point with the line up checks already complete. The spacing produced was precise enough that No2 joined with minimal power changes and no correction from the leader.
texts.marginal: SP released brakes within the briefed interval, but the line up work was completed so close to that point that the timing was set with little margin. The spacing achieved was correct and No2 joined without difficulty, yet a further delay in the checks would have moved the release outside the plan. SP is expected to complete the pre-takeoff work earlier so that the interval is chosen rather than accepted.

texts_at.1: SP set brake release outside the briefed spacing and adjusted it only after the IP called for the correct interval, with the leader's own airspeed then running about 10 knots above standard in the climb, because the line-up checks ran unfinished into the takeoff clearance. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to finish the checks before the clearance so the interval is chosen rather than accepted.
texts_at.2: SP recognized a brake release that did not match the briefed interval and adjusted the timing without prompting, with the resulting airspeed excess in the climb reaching roughly 7 knots, because the line-up workload had concentrated into the last part of the sequence. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to spread the line-up workload earlier so the release point does not need a late correction.
texts_at.3: SP held the climb airspeed within 5 knots of standard while releasing brakes within the briefed interval, with the line-up work finished close enough to that point to leave little margin on one departure. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the line-up work with more margin ahead of the briefed release point.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a brake release outside the briefed spacing and adjusted the timing without prompting, holding the resulting airspeed excess in the climb to about 7 knots. Weighing the wind, the turn and the spacing together before taxi, rather than at the line, would remove the need for that adjustment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good timing of the pre-takeoff workload.
texts_above.3: SP took into account the crosswind, the departure turn and the briefed spacing and released brakes at the planned point, with the climb airspeed held inside 5 knots of standard and No2 given a straightforward join-up. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good timing of the pre-takeoff workload.
texts_above.4: SP set the interval from a complete assessment of wind, turn and traffic and released brakes exactly at the briefed point with the line-up checks already complete, so No2 joined with minimal power change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent timing of the pre-takeoff workload.

error_modes.label: Interval T/O - monitoring of No2 and leader climb management for the join-up

texts.0: SP, due to attention held entirely on the leader's own departure profile, did not effectively monitor No2 during the interval T/O. The wingman's late roll and slow acceleration went unobserved, no power or track adjustment was made by the leader, and the leader's own climb speed was at the same time more than 10 knots above the standard. IP intervened on the controls and on the radio to re-establish a workable join-up geometry.
texts.1: SP, due to a departure flown without any allocation of scan to the wingman, did not effectively monitor No2 after lift-off. The developing spacing problem was recognized only after two calls from IP, by which time the leader's climb speed sat about 10 knots above the standard at the limit of the allowed tolerance. The join-up was completed with the whole correction carried out by No2.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that reached the wingman late in the initial climb, monitored No2 only intermittently after lift-off. The lapse allowed the leader's own climb speed to run roughly 7 knots above the standard, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before SP re-established the check on No2, reset the power and stabilized the profile without prompting.
texts.3: SP effectively monitored No2 during the interval T/O, checking the wingman's roll, lift-off and closure while holding the leader's own parameters within standards. Small power and heading adjustments were made in time to keep the join-up on the briefed geometry.
texts.4: SP monitored No2 continuously from brake release through the join-up, integrating the wingman into the scan with no loss of precision on the leader's own parameters. The climb was flown so that the closure remained comfortable for the wingman at every stage.
texts.marginal: SP monitored No2 during the interval T/O, but the checks were spaced widely and the wingman's position was confirmed mainly at lift-off and again at the start of the join-up. All parameters stayed within standards on this departure, yet a change in the closure between those points would have been seen late. SP is expected to keep the wingman inside a continuous scan through the whole join-up.

texts_at.1: SP recognized the developing spacing problem only after being prompted, with the leader's own climb speed by then about 10 knots above standard at the tolerance limit, because the scan had not yet been divided to include the wingman. texts_above.2: SP re-established the check on No2 and reset the climb power without prompting, holding the leader's own airspeed excess to about 7 knots while the profile was stabilized. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound scan coverage through the join-up.
texts_above.3: SP checked the wingman's roll, lift-off and closure while holding the leader's own climb speed inside 5 knots of standard, with small adjustments made in time to keep the join-up on the briefed geometry. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed scan coverage through the join-up.
texts_above.4: SP monitored No2 continuously from brake release through the join-up with no loss of precision on the leader's own climb parameters, flying the climb so the closure stayed comfortable for the wingman at every stage. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional scan coverage through the join-up.

error_modes.label: Interval T/O - gear retraction command after No2 is confirmed airborne

texts.0: SP, due to a configuration call driven by the leader's own climb rather than by the state of the wingman, gave the command for landing gear retraction without confirming that No2 was safely airborne. No2 was still on the runway in the takeoff roll when the call was passed, and the leader's own airspeed was more than 10 knots above the standard. IP cancelled the command on the radio and took the controls to stabilize the departure.
texts.1: SP, due to a fixed cadence carried over from single-ship departures, passed the gear retraction command before the state of No2 had been confirmed. The call was corrected only after IP prompted for the wingman, and during the exchange the leader's airspeed sat at about 10 knots above the standard at the limit of the allowed tolerance. The formation was reconfigured late and the join-up started from a degraded geometry.
texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on the leader's own climb parameters, started the gear retraction call before the check on No2 was complete. SP stopped the call on his own initiative, confirmed that No2 was safely airborne and then passed the command, with the leader's airspeed excess reaching roughly 7 knots between the code 3 and code 1 limits during the pause. No prompting and no IP input were required.
texts.3: SP confirmed that No2 was safely airborne before giving the command for landing gear retraction, checking the wingman's lift-off and climb and only then passing the call. The command was standard and timed so that both aircraft were clean before the departure turn.
texts.4: SP confirmed No2 safely airborne with a positive check and passed the gear retraction command at exactly the required point, without any degradation of the leader's own climb parameters. Both aircraft were configured on a stable flight path and the join-up was begun clean.
texts.marginal: SP confirmed that No2 was airborne before commanding gear retraction, but the check was brief and the command followed almost at once. Nothing was omitted on this departure, yet the margin between the check and the call was minimal for an interval takeoff where the wingman is well behind. SP is expected to make the confirmation of No2 deliberate before passing the command.

texts_at.1: SP passed the gear-up call before the check on No2 was complete and corrected it only after being prompted, with the leader's own airspeed sitting about 10 knots above standard during the exchange, because the command cadence carried over from single-ship departures. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to build a positive check on No2 into the interval departure before the call is made.
texts_at.2: SP stopped an early gear-up call without prompting to confirm No2 safely airborne, with the leader's own airspeed excess reaching roughly 7 knots during the pause, because attention had settled first on the leader's own climb parameters. texts_at.3: SP held the climb airspeed within 5 knots of standard while checking that No2 was safely airborne before each gear-up call, with the confirmation brief rather than deliberate on one departure. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make that one confirmation as unhurried as the rest.

texts_above.2: SP interrupted an early call to confirm No2 airborne, holding the leader's own airspeed excess to about 7 knots while the sequence was corrected without prompting. texts_above.3: SP confirmed No2 safely airborne before every gear-up call on the interval departure, with the leader's own airspeed held inside 5 knots of standard and no call needing correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed confirmation before the gear-up call.
texts_above.4: SP passed the gear-up command at exactly the required point, on a positive check of No2 that never degraded the leader's own climb parameters, leaving both aircraft configured clean before the join-up. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding confirmation before the gear-up call.

error_modes.label: Lineup check completion before brake release (NILTAP)

texts.0: SP, due to the lineup check being started only after the aircraft was already creeping forward instead of after the complete stop on the centerline of the active runway, did not complete the NILTAP items before brake release. NWS was left engaged after the aircraft was aligned with the runway and the panel was not clear, and the swing that followed carried the aircraft more than 10 feet off the assigned takeoff line toward the half of the runway occupied by No2. IP took the controls to stop the divergence and to complete the configuration.
texts.1: SP, due to lineup check items being called from memory instead of the BOTH items being confirmed with the PNF, left part of the NILTAP sequence unfinished when the takeoff clearance was accepted. Landing light and taxi light were set only after IP called for them, and the distraction let the aircraft drift about 10 feet from the takeoff line, at the limit of the allowed deviation. The pair rolled with the configuration completed late and with No2 adjusting to preserve spacing.
texts.2: SP, due to the lineup check being run while the aircraft was still being aligned rather than after the stop on the centerline, initially missed the NWS deselection item. SP caught the omission against the NILTAP sequence before brake release and deselected NWS on his own initiative, with the residual deviation from the takeoff line reaching roughly 8 feet between the code 3 and code 1 limits. No prompting and no IP action were required.
texts.3: SP stopped the aircraft on the centerline of the active runway and completed the lineup check in full before brake release, running NILTAP with NWS deselected after alignment, IFF NORMAL, landing and taxi lights on, ANTICE on and the panel clear. Final was cleared prior to crossing the runway hold short line and the takeoff line was then held inside 5 feet.
texts.4: SP completed the lineup check without hesitation, confirming every BOTH item with the PNF and reporting the panel clear with only ANTI ICE on, well before the takeoff clearance. The aircraft was correctly configured at brake release and the takeoff line was held with deviations barely perceptible against the runway markings.
texts.marginal: SP completed all NILTAP items before brake release, but the sequence was finished so close to the clearance that the last items were compressed and the confirmation with the PNF was reduced to a single call. Nothing was left unset and the takeoff line stayed within standards, yet a further delay would have pushed an item past brake release. SP is expected to stop on the centerline and complete the check with margin instead of compressing it into the clearance.

texts_at.1: SP completed the NILTAP sequence with the takeoff line displaced to about 10 feet, at the tolerance limit, because two items were confirmed from memory rather than checked BOTH with the PNF before the stop was complete. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to run the BOTH items against the PNF call rather than from memory so the sequence does not compress toward brake release.
texts_at.2: SP completed the NILTAP sequence with the takeoff line held to roughly 8 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the check was started while the aircraft was still being aligned rather than after the complete stop on the centerline. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to wait for the full stop before starting the check so the line does not open before NWS is deselected.
texts_at.3: SP completed the NILTAP sequence and held the takeoff line inside 5 feet on three of the four line ups, with the fourth check finished close enough to the clearance that the PNF confirmation was reduced to a single call. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep the same margin on every line up that the first three showed.

texts_above.2: SP stopped on the centerline, ran the NILTAP sequence and still held the takeoff line to about 8 feet before rotation, catching the residual drift without prompting. Stopping fully before the first item is called, rather than as the aircraft settles, would close even that margin. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable checklist discipline before brake release.
texts_above.3: SP stopped the aircraft on the centerline, ran the complete NILTAP sequence with every BOTH item confirmed against the PNF and held the takeoff line inside 5 feet through rotation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate checklist discipline before brake release.
texts_above.4: SP completed the NILTAP sequence without hesitation, confirming every BOTH item and reporting the panel clear well before the clearance, with the takeoff line held to a couple of feet at most. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary checklist discipline before brake release.

error_modes.label: Aircraft creep during the static takeoff engine run-up

texts.0: SP, due to the brakes not being pumped up before the engine run-up, allowed the aircraft to creep while the PCL was advanced to 25 to 30 percent torque for the static takeoff. The creep was not detected because the crosscheck stayed inside on the engine instruments instead of going outside, and the aircraft moved off the assigned takeoff line by more than 10 feet toward No2 before brake release. IP took the controls and stopped the aircraft to re-establish the runway alignment.
texts.1: SP, due to a run-up begun without pumping the brakes up, allowed the aircraft to creep at 25 to 30 percent torque during the static takeoff. The movement was recognized only after IP called it out, by which time the displacement from the takeoff line had reached about 10 feet, at the limit of the allowed deviation. The takeoff roll was then started from a position that had to be corrected during the acceleration.
texts.2: SP, due to brakes pumped up only partially before advancing the PCL to 25 to 30 percent torque, let a slow creep begin during the static run-up. SP detected the movement on the outside crosscheck, held the aircraft and re-established the alignment without prompting, with the maximum displacement from the takeoff line reaching roughly 7 feet between the code 3 and code 1 limits. No IP action was required.
texts.3: SP pumped up the brakes before the static run-up and held the aircraft stationary while the PCL was advanced to 25 to 30 percent torque, crosschecking outside to detect creep as well as reading the engine instruments. The aircraft stayed on the assigned takeoff line inside 5 feet and brake release was taken from the briefed position.
texts.4: SP set brake pressure so that no movement was possible at run-up torque and alternated the crosscheck between the runway ahead and the engine instruments throughout. The aircraft did not move perceptibly on the takeoff line and brake release was taken from exactly the briefed position alongside No2.
texts.marginal: SP held the aircraft during the run-up and the takeoff line stayed within standards, but the brakes were pumped up late and the aircraft settled a small distance forward before the pressure took effect. The displacement did not grow and did not affect the pair, yet it was accepted rather than removed. SP is expected to pump the brakes up before advancing the PCL so that creep is prevented rather than detected.

texts_at.1: SP held the aircraft during the run-up with the displacement from the takeoff line reaching about 10 feet, at the tolerance limit, because the brakes were pumped up only after the PCL had already been advanced toward 25 to 30 percent torque. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to pump the brakes up before the PCL is advanced so the aircraft does not need to be re-centered.
texts_at.2: SP held the aircraft during the run-up with the takeoff line displacement reaching roughly 7 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the outside crosscheck was slower to pick up the creep than the engine instrument scan. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to alternate the scan outside more often during the run-up so the creep is caught at its onset.
texts_at.3: SP held the aircraft inside 5 feet of the takeoff line on three of the four run-ups, with the fourth showing a small forward settle before the brake pressure fully took effect. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to pump the brakes up earlier so every run-up matches the first three.

texts_above.2: SP detected the creep developing during the run-up and held the takeoff line to about 7 feet, re-establishing the alignment without prompting before the run-up was complete. Pumping the brakes up before the PCL is advanced, rather than after, would remove the creep altogether. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady brake and crosscheck discipline during the run-up.
texts_above.3: SP pumped the brakes up before the static run-up and crosschecked outside through the advance to 25 to 30 percent torque, holding the takeoff line inside 5 feet with no creep the wingman could see. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good brake and crosscheck discipline during the run-up.
texts_above.4: SP set brake pressure so firmly that no movement was possible at run-up torque, alternating the scan between the runway ahead and the engine instruments with the takeoff line unchanged to within a foot or two. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior brake and crosscheck discipline during the run-up.

error_modes.label: Engine instrument check when stabilized at maximum power

texts.0: SP, due to attention transferred entirely to No2 as soon as the PCL reached MAX, did not check the engine instruments when stabilized at maximum power, approximately 3 seconds after the advance. The takeoff roll was continued with engine operation unverified and the scan returned late to the runway, letting the aircraft depart the takeoff line by more than 10 feet toward the wingman. IP intervened on the controls to restore the track and to confirm the engine indications.
texts.1: SP, due to the PCL being advanced with the scan going straight outside, omitted the engine instrument check at maximum power until IP called for it. The check was made well after the 3 second point and the delay left the takeoff line offset by about 10 feet, at the limit of the allowed deviation, before the correction took effect. The pair lifted off with the track still being recovered.
texts.2: SP, due to a check attempted before the indications had stabilized at maximum power, read the engine instruments too early and had to return to them during the acceleration. The second read was taken on SP's own initiative and confirmed proper operation, with the deviation from the takeoff line produced by the divided attention reaching roughly 7 feet between the code 3 and code 1 limits. No prompting and no IP action were needed.
texts.3: SP smoothly advanced the PCL to MAX and checked the engine instruments when stabilized at maximum power, approximately 3 seconds after the PCL reached the stop, confirming proper operation before committing to the roll. The takeoff line was held inside 5 feet while the check was made.
texts.4: SP timed the engine instrument check exactly to the stabilization of maximum power and completed it in a single short read, without any loss of runway alignment or of the picture of No2. Deviations from the takeoff line during the check were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP checked the engine instruments at maximum power and confirmed proper operation, but the check was taken as one long look inside rather than a brief read integrated into the outside scan. All parameters stayed within standards, yet the runway and the wingman were unattended for longer than necessary. SP is expected to keep the check short at the 3 second point and return the scan outside immediately.

texts_at.1: SP checked the engine instruments only after IP prompted for it, by which point the takeoff line had opened to about 10 feet, at the tolerance limit, because the PCL advance to MAX was flown with the scan going straight outside and no plan to return to the gauges. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to time the instrument check to the 3 second stabilization point so the scan returns outside before the line opens.
texts_at.2: SP read the engine instruments at maximum power with the takeoff line displaced roughly 7 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the first attempt at the check was made before the indications had stabilized and had to be repeated. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to wait for the 3 second stabilization point before reading the gauges so the check is not repeated.
texts_at.3: SP held the takeoff line inside 5 feet while checking the engine instruments at maximum power on three of the four takeoffs, with the fourth check taken a beat before the indications had fully settled. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that same timing on every takeoff.

texts_above.2: SP checked the engine instruments at maximum power and still held the takeoff line to about 7 feet, correcting the divided attention without prompting once the second read confirmed proper operation. Timing the single read to the 3 second stabilization point, rather than checking early and again late, would remove that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured engine instrument crosscheck at maximum power.
texts_above.3: SP advanced the PCL smoothly to MAX and checked the engine instruments at the 3 second stabilization point in a single read, holding the takeoff line inside 5 feet throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise engine instrument crosscheck at maximum power.
texts_above.4: SP timed the engine instrument check exactly to the stabilization of maximum power and completed it in one short look with no loss of runway alignment, the takeoff line moving only a foot or two during the check. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate engine instrument crosscheck at maximum power.

error_modes.label: Elevator position during the takeoff roll and nose gear loading

texts.0: SP, due to forward stick held through the acceleration instead of an elevator positioned approximately neutral, loaded the nose gear so that it dug in during the takeoff roll. Directional control became heavy on the rudder, the aircraft wandered off the assigned takeoff line by more than 10 feet, and the late rotation that followed carried the takeoff airspeed more than 10 knots past the standard. IP took the controls to unload the nose gear and to re-establish the track and the speed.
texts.1: SP, due to an elevator that was not held approximately neutral during the takeoff roll, allowed the nose gear to dig in and the steering to become heavy. The pressure was relaxed only after IP called for a neutral elevator, and the takeoff airspeed at lift-off then sat about 10 knots above the standard, at the outer limit of the one-sided tolerance. The pair lifted off with the leader fast and No2 correcting with power.
texts.2: SP, due to slight forward pressure carried into the initial acceleration, loaded the nose gear more than required before recognizing that the elevator was not approximately neutral. SP relaxed the pressure on his own initiative and restored normal rudder steering, with the airspeed excess produced by the slightly late rotation reaching roughly 7 knots between the code 3 and code 1 limits. No prompting and no IP input were needed.
texts.3: SP positioned the elevator approximately neutral during the takeoff roll so that the nose gear did not dig in and directional control remained on the rudder. Rotation was made at the computed speed and the takeoff airspeed excess was held inside 5 knots.
texts.4: SP held the elevator approximately neutral throughout the acceleration with no perceptible loading of the nose gear, so that rudder steering stayed light and precise. Rotation was taken exactly at the computed speed with negligible deviation in takeoff airspeed.
texts.marginal: SP kept the elevator close to neutral and the nose gear was not dug in, but the position drifted slightly forward as the acceleration built and was reset only once the aircraft felt heavy on the rudder. All parameters remained within standards, yet the tendency reappeared with each application of power. SP is expected to set an approximately neutral elevator at brake release and hold it for the whole roll.

texts_at.1: SP held the elevator away from neutral long enough that the nose gear dug in, and the late rotation that followed left the takeoff airspeed about 10 knots above standard, at the tolerance limit, because the pressure was relaxed only once the aircraft already felt heavy on the rudder. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set an approximately neutral elevator at brake release so the nose gear never loads enough to delay the rotation.
texts_at.2: SP carried slight forward pressure into the acceleration and the resulting late rotation left the takeoff airspeed roughly 7 knots above standard, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the elevator was not recognized as off neutral until the steering had already become heavy. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the elevator position earlier in the roll so the nose gear does not load before the correction is made.
texts_at.3: SP held the takeoff airspeed inside 5 knots of standard on three of the four takeoffs with the elevator approximately neutral, the fourth showing a trace of forward pressure that was corrected before it affected the steering. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same neutral elevator on every takeoff that the first three showed.

texts_above.2: SP relaxed a slight forward pressure once the nose gear loading was recognized, holding the resulting airspeed excess to about 7 knots and restoring normal rudder steering without prompting. Setting the elevator neutral at brake release, rather than correcting it once the steering goes heavy, would remove that excess. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent elevator control during the takeoff roll.
texts_above.3: SP positioned the elevator approximately neutral through the takeoff roll so the nose gear never dug in, rotating at the computed speed with the airspeed excess held inside 5 knots. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined elevator control during the takeoff roll.
texts_above.4: SP held the elevator approximately neutral throughout the acceleration with no perceptible nose gear loading, so the rudder steering stayed light and the rotation came in within a knot or two of the computed speed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding elevator control during the takeoff roll.

error_modes.label: Aileron into the wind and prevention of skipping on a crosswind takeoff

texts.0: SP, due to aileron neither prepositioned into the wind nor applied as required during the roll, let the upwind wing develop more lift and begin flying before the downwind wing. Skipping developed, with the aircraft moving sideways in a series of very small bounces and increased stress on the landing gear, and the takeoff line was exceeded by more than 10 feet toward the half of the runway occupied by No2. IP took the controls to level the wings and to re-establish the takeoff track.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient aileron into the crosswind component, allowed the upwind wing to rise during the takeoff roll and the first indications of skipping to appear. The wings were leveled only after IP called for aileron into the wind, and the sideways movement left the aircraft about 10 feet from the takeoff line, at the limit of the allowed deviation.
texts.2: SP, due to aileron applied reactively instead of being prepositioned into the wind, allowed the upwind wing to start rising early in the roll. SP recognized the tendency, increased aileron into the crosswind component before any bounce developed and re-centered the aircraft, with the maximum lateral deviation reaching roughly 8 feet between the code 3 and code 1 limits. No prompting and no IP action were required.
texts.3: SP prepositioned aileron into the wind and adjusted it as required during the takeoff roll, keeping the wings level with no tendency of the upwind wing to fly first and no skipping. Rudder was used to prevent the aircraft from weather-vaning and the takeoff line was held inside 5 feet through rotation.
texts.4: SP matched the aileron continuously to the crosswind so that the wings stayed level throughout the roll with no sideways movement at any point. The takeoff track was held with deviations barely perceptible and gave No2 a stable reference for the whole acceleration.
texts.marginal: SP kept the wings level and no skipping occurred, but the aileron was set slightly less than the crosswind demanded and the upwind wing showed a light tendency to rise late in the roll. The deviation stayed within standards and lift-off was normal, yet the margin against a bounce was small. SP is expected to anticipate the aileron requirement and preposition it into the wind before brake release.

texts_at.1: SP allowed the upwind wing to rise and the first signs of skipping to appear before applying aileron into the crosswind, and the sideways movement left the aircraft about 10 feet from the takeoff line, at the tolerance limit, because the correction was reactive rather than prepositioned. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to preposition aileron into the wind before brake release so the upwind wing does not begin to rise.
texts_at.2: SP applied aileron reactively rather than prepositioning it into the wind, and the upwind wing's early rise carried the aircraft roughly 8 feet off the takeoff line, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the crosswind aileron correction before the throttle is advanced so the wing does not start to rise at all.
texts_at.3: SP held the takeoff line inside 5 feet with the wings level on three of the four crosswind takeoffs, the fourth showing a light tendency of the upwind wing to rise late in the roll before the aileron was increased. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to match the aileron input on every takeoff to the one that held the first three level.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the upwind wing beginning to rise and increased aileron into the crosswind before any bounce developed, holding the lateral deviation to about 8 feet without prompting. Prepositioning the aileron into the wind at brake release, rather than reacting to the first rise, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound crosswind aileron technique.
texts_above.3: SP prepositioned aileron into the wind and adjusted it through the roll so the wings stayed level with no tendency to skip, holding the takeoff line inside 5 feet through rotation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed crosswind aileron technique.
texts_above.4: SP matched the aileron continuously to the crosswind so the wings stayed level for the whole roll with no sideways movement at any point, the takeoff line moving only a foot or two throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional crosswind aileron technique.

error_modes.label: Establishment of the takeoff attitude at rotation

texts.0: SP, due to backstick pressure applied abruptly rather than smoothly at rotation speed, set a pitch well beyond the 7 to 10 degree nose high takeoff attitude. The aircraft left the runway steeply, the attitude was then reversed to recover the picture, and the airspeed swung more than 10 knots past the standard while No2 lost a usable reference on the leader. IP took the controls to establish the takeoff attitude and stabilize the initial climb.
texts.1: SP, due to a rotation flown by feel instead of against the takeoff attitude picture, established a pitch outside the 7 to 10 degree band and carried it into the initial climb. The attitude was corrected only after IP called the pitch, and the airspeed excess produced by the chase settled at about 10 knots, at the outer limit of the one-sided tolerance. No2 was obliged to change power to hold position.
texts.2: SP, due to backstick pressure that was slightly too rapid at rotation speed, over-rotated past the upper end of the 7 to 10 degree takeoff attitude. SP reduced the pitch attitude picture by half, placing the spinner slightly below the horizon, and restored the takeoff attitude without prompting, with the airspeed excess reaching roughly 7 knots between the code 3 and code 1 limits.
texts.3: SP applied smooth backstick pressure at rotation speed and established the takeoff attitude of approximately 7 to 10 degrees nose high, holding it with control stick pressure through lift-off. The takeoff airspeed excess stayed inside 5 knots and the flight path presented to No2 was steady.
texts.4: SP set the takeoff attitude in one smooth movement and held the spinner picture unchanged from lift-off into the initial climb, with negligible deviation in takeoff airspeed. The pitch was stable enough that No2 flew the join-up with minimal power changes.
texts.marginal: SP established the takeoff attitude inside the 7 to 10 degree band, but at its upper edge, and held it with continuous small corrections rather than with steady stick pressure on a fixed picture. Airspeed stayed within standards and No2 held position, yet the attitude was maintained by chasing rather than by holding a reference. SP is expected to set the takeoff attitude on the spinner reference and hold it with steady pressure.

texts_at.1: SP established the takeoff attitude by feel rather than against the 7 to 10 degree picture, and the chase that followed left the takeoff airspeed about 10 knots above standard, at the tolerance limit, until the pitch was corrected on the called reference. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the attitude on the spinner reference at rotation rather than adjusting it once the airspeed has already drifted.
texts_at.2: SP over-rotated slightly past the upper end of the 7 to 10 degree takeoff attitude at a rotation speed that was applied a little too rapidly, and the resulting airspeed excess reached roughly 7 knots, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the backstick pressure more smoothly at rotation speed so the attitude is captured on the first movement.
texts_at.3: SP held the takeoff airspeed inside 5 knots of standard on three of the four rotations with the attitude set at approximately 7 to 10 degrees nose high, the fourth needing a small correction after the initial pitch settled a touch high. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the same picture on every rotation that the first three showed.

texts_above.2: SP reduced an over-rotated attitude picture back toward the 7 to 10 degree band without prompting, holding the resulting airspeed excess to about 7 knots while the takeoff attitude was restored. Applying smooth backstick pressure at rotation speed, rather than correcting an over-rotation afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable takeoff attitude control at rotation.
texts_above.3: SP applied smooth backstick pressure at rotation speed and established the takeoff attitude at approximately 7 to 10 degrees nose high, holding it through lift-off with the airspeed excess inside 5 knots. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed takeoff attitude control at rotation.
texts_above.4: SP set the takeoff attitude in one smooth movement and held the spinner picture unchanged from lift-off into the climb, with the airspeed staying within a knot or two of standard. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding takeoff attitude control at rotation.

error_modes.label: Right rudder trim after takeoff and safe gear retraction

texts.0: SP, due to the trim work being deferred while attention stayed on the wingman, did not apply right rudder trim immediately after takeoff and safe gear retraction. Adverse yaw was left uncompensated with the ball well off center, the aircraft was flown out of balance on continuous foot pressure, and the associated speed control error carried the climb airspeed more than 10 knots above the standard held for No2. IP took the controls, trimmed the aircraft and re-established the departure parameters.
texts.1: SP, due to a departure flown with the feet holding the yaw instead of the trim taking it, left the ball off center after gear retraction. Right rudder trim was applied only after IP called for it, and while the aircraft was out of balance the climb airspeed sat about 10 knots above the standard, at the limit of the allowed tolerance. No2 had to correct across the turn to hold position.
texts.2: SP, due to right rudder trim applied later than the safe gear retraction point, flew part of the initial climb with the ball slightly off center. SP recognized the out of balance condition, trimmed the yaw out on his own initiative and reset the speed, with the airspeed excess reaching roughly 7 knots between the code 3 and code 1 limits. No prompting and no IP input were needed.
texts.3: SP applied right rudder trim immediately after takeoff and safe gear retraction, centering the ball and removing the adverse yaw so that the aircraft was flown without residual pressure. Climb airspeed was held inside 5 knots of the standard and the flight path stayed steady for No2.
texts.4: SP trimmed the yaw out as soon as the gear was safely retracted, keeping the ball centered with no residual foot pressure at any stage of the climb. Airspeed deviations were negligible and the leader presented a stable platform for the join-up.
texts.marginal: SP applied right rudder trim after safe gear retraction and the ball ended up centered, but the trim was set in one late input and small foot pressure was carried until then. Parameters stayed within standards and the wingman was not affected, yet the aircraft was flown out of balance longer than necessary. SP is expected to trim the yaw out immediately after gear retraction so that the climb starts in balance.

texts_at.1: SP flew part of the initial climb with the ball off center after gear retraction, and the airspeed correction made while out of balance settled about 10 knots above standard, at the tolerance limit, until IP called for the trim to be applied. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply right rudder trim immediately on safe gear retraction so the climb starts in balance.
texts_at.2: SP carried the ball slightly off center into part of the initial climb before recognizing that right rudder trim had not been applied, and the airspeed excess produced while out of balance reached roughly 7 knots, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to trim the yaw out at the same moment the gear is confirmed up so the climb does not begin out of balance.
texts_at.3: SP held the climb airspeed inside 5 knots of standard with the ball centered on three of the four climbs, the fourth carrying a trace of foot pressure before the trim was set. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the trim on every climb as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the aircraft out of balance after gear retraction and trimmed the yaw out without prompting, holding the resulting airspeed excess to about 7 knots while the correction was made. Applying right rudder trim the moment the gear is confirmed up, rather than once the ball is already off center, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid trim technique after gear retraction.
texts_above.3: SP applied right rudder trim immediately after takeoff and safe gear retraction, centering the ball with no residual pressure and holding the climb airspeed inside 5 knots of standard. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate trim technique after gear retraction.
texts_above.4: SP trimmed the yaw out as soon as the gear was safely retracted, keeping the ball centered with no residual foot pressure and the airspeed staying within a knot or two of standard. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless trim technique after gear retraction.

error_modes.label: Interval T/O - head nod confirming No2 run-up complete before brake release

texts.0: SP, due to waiting for a visual signal that does not exist for the interval takeoff, released brakes before No2's head nod confirmed that the engine run-up check was complete. The wingman was still at run-up torque when the leader rolled, the 10 second interval was therefore never established, and airborne the leader held more than 10 knots above the 160 KIAS to be maintained at 85 percent power. IP intervened on the radio and on the controls to rebuild the departure.
texts.1: SP, due to the run-up phase being closed on the leader's own clock rather than on the wingman's acknowledgment, released brakes without positively taking No2's head nod. The omission was pointed out by IP after the roll had begun, and the leader then stabilized about 10 knots above the 160 KIAS held at 85 percent power, at the limit of the allowed tolerance. No2 rolled late and the rejoin was flown with a geometry the wingman had to correct.
texts.2: SP, due to the check on the wingman being made with a quick glance instead of a deliberate look for the head nod, began to release brakes before the acknowledgment was clearly seen. SP held the aircraft, confirmed the head nod that the run-up check was complete and then performed the MAX power takeoff, with the excess above 160 KIAS reaching roughly 7 knots between the code 3 and code 1 limits. No prompting and no IP action were required.
texts.3: SP waited for No2's head nod confirming that the engine run-up check was complete, then released brakes and performed the MAX power takeoff, with No2 rolling 10 seconds later. Airborne at a minimum of 160 KIAS, SP reduced power to 85 percent and held the airspeed inside 5 knots of that figure.
texts.4: SP took the head nod deliberately, knowing that no visual signal exists for the interval takeoff, and released brakes exactly at the briefed point. Power was reduced to 85 percent as soon as the aircraft was airborne at 160 KIAS and the airspeed was held with negligible deviation, giving No2 a predictable rejoin.
texts.marginal: SP confirmed No2's head nod before brake release and the interval was correct, but the check was taken almost simultaneously with the release rather than as a separate step. Nothing was missed and the climb airspeed stayed within standards, yet a delayed nod from the wingman would have been seen only after the roll had started. SP is expected to separate the acknowledgment from the brake release so that the confirmation clearly precedes it.

texts_at.1: SP released brakes without positively taking No2's head nod, and once airborne the airspeed stabilized about 10 knots above the 160 KIAS held at 85 percent power, at the tolerance limit, until IP pointed out the missed confirmation. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to take the head nod as a deliberate, separate step before brake release rather than closing the run-up phase on the leader's own clock.
texts_at.2: SP checked the wingman's head nod with a quick glance rather than a deliberate look, and the resulting airspeed above 160 KIAS reached roughly 7 knots, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before the power reduction to 85 percent was completed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the aircraft until the head nod is clearly seen so the power reduction is not started against an unconfirmed signal.
texts_at.3: SP held the climb airspeed inside 5 knots of the 160 KIAS reference on three of the four interval takeoffs after confirming No2's head nod, the fourth needing a small correction once the power reduction to 85 percent lagged the airspeed by a moment. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to reduce power at 160 KIAS as consistently as the first three departures showed.

texts_above.2: SP confirmed the head nod deliberately, knowing no visual signal exists for the interval takeoff, and still held the airspeed above 160 KIAS to about 7 knots while the power reduction to 85 percent was completed without prompting. Reducing power the instant 160 KIAS is reached, rather than a moment after, would trim that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good power and airspeed management on the interval departure.
texts_above.3: SP waited for No2's head nod, released brakes and performed the MAX power takeoff, reducing to 85 percent as soon as the aircraft was airborne at 160 KIAS and holding the airspeed inside 5 knots of that figure. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good power and airspeed management on the interval departure.
texts_above.4: SP took the head nod deliberately and released brakes at exactly the briefed point, reducing power to 85 percent as soon as the aircraft was airborne at 160 KIAS and holding the airspeed within a knot or two of that figure. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent power and airspeed management on the interval departure.
